cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="18" y1="90" x2="242" y2="90" class="gk"/><line x1="38" y1="62" x2="38" y2="118" class="lk"/><line x1="14" y1="90" x2="62" y2="90" class="lk"/><line x1="20" y1="72" x2="56" y2="108" class="ik"/><line x1="20" y1="108" x2="56" y2="72" class="ik"/><rect x="92" y="36" width="18" height="108" rx="4" class="s ok"/><line x1="101" y1="46" x2="101" y2="134" class="lk"/><line x1="144" y1="56" x2="144" y2="124" class="lk"/><rect x="184" y="58" width="42" height="64" rx="4" class="s ok"/><line x1="192" y1="90" x2="218" y2="90" class="ik"/><text x="38" y="142" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Unpolarised</text><text x="101" y="28" text-anchor="middle" class="t">P₁ (Polariser)</text><text x="144" y="46" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Linear E</text><text x="205" y="48" text-anchor="middle" class="t">P₂ (Analyser)</text><text x="205" y="142" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Crossed → 0</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at unpolarised light (left star) passing P₁ to become vertically polarised, then blocked when analyser P₂ is turned horizontal.
cards.example: If light were a longitudinal wave (vibrating along z), rotating the second Polaroid P₂ would never change the transmitted brightness.
cards.bridge: In Maxwell's electromagnetic wave along z, E (along x) and H (along y) are both perpendicular to z, with E_z = H_z = 0.

cards.label: 03 · §22.1 Definition
cards.title: What is unpolarised light and a Polaroid pass axis?
cards.body: In unpolarised light, the transverse electric vector E changes direction randomly. A Polaroid absorbs E along one axis and transmits E along its perpendicular pass axis.
cards.tex: E_x = E_0\cos(kz - \omega t), \quad H_y = H_0\cos(kz - \omega t), \quad E_z = H_z = 0

cards.label: 04 · §22.1 Electromagnetic wave
cards.title: Transverse electric and magnetic fields in a dielectric (Eqs. 22.4–22.8)
cards.body: For an \(x\)-polarised plane wave propagating along \(+z\) (along \(\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{H}\)), \(\mathbf{E}\) lies along \(x\), \(\mathbf{H}\) lies along \(y\), and the intrinsic impedance of free space is \(\eta_0 \approx 120\pi\,\Omega\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Which property of light is proved when rotating a second Polaroid causes darkness?
cards.why: Only a transverse wave changes its transmitted amplitude when the orientation of a slit or Polaroid is rotated (§22.1).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In an electromagnetic wave with \(\mathbf{E}\) along \(x\) and \(\mathbf{H}\) along \(y\), light travels along:
cards.why: Vectors \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{H}\) are perpendicular to each other and the wave propagates along \(\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{H}\) (§22.1).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: The direction of the electric vector transmitted by a Polaroid is called its ______ axis.
cards.why: A Polaroid absorbs the component of \(\mathbf{E}\) along one direction and transmits the perpendicular component along its pass axis (§22.1).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: A circularly polarised wave on a string has amplitude \(a = 3\text{ cm}\). Find \(x^2 + y^2\) in \(\text{cm}^2\).

sheets.title: Production of polarised light
sheets.source: Unit 18 · Ghatak ch. 22 §22.3 (PDF pp. 358–360; Book 2 not available); syllabus item 18

cards.title: Why parallel wires block the electric component parallel to them
cards.meaning: A wire-grid polariser or Polaroid sheet uses parallel conducting lines that let electrons slide along them, absorbing the parallel electric field as heat.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="18" y1="90" x2="242" y2="90" class="gk"/><line x1="42" y1="56" x2="42" y2="124" class="lk"/><line x1="16" y1="90" x2="68" y2="90" class="ik"/><rect x="102" y="28" width="48" height="124" rx="4" class="s ok"/><line x1="112" y1="28" x2="112" y2="152" class="ik"/><line x1="122" y1="28" x2="122" y2="152" class="ik"/><line x1="132" y1="28" x2="132" y2="152" class="ik"/><line x1="142" y1="28" x2="142" y2="152" class="ik"/><line x1="182" y1="90" x2="234" y2="90" class="lk"/><circle cx="182" cy="90" r="3" class="f"/><circle cx="234" cy="90" r="3" class="f"/><text x="42" y="46" text-anchor="middle" class="t">E_x and E_y</text><text x="126" y="20" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Wires along y (E_y absorbed)</text><text x="208" y="72" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Emergent E_x</text><text x="208" y="114" text-anchor="middle" class="t">(Pass axis ⊥ wires)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the vertical wires along y: the vertical E_y drives currents in the wires and is absorbed, while horizontal E_x passes through.
cards.example: A 3 cm microwave wire grid is easy to build because wire spacing only needs to be less than 3 cm; for visible light, a Polaroid uses aligned iodine polymer chains.
cards.bridge: Therefore the pass axis of a wire-grid polariser or Polaroid is always perpendicular to the aligned conducting wires or polymer molecules.

cards.label: 01 · §22.3.1 Definition
cards.title: What are a wire-grid polariser and a Polaroid?
cards.body: A wire-grid polariser has parallel wires spaced less than λ that absorb E parallel to the wires by Joule heating and transmit E perpendicular. A Polaroid uses aligned iodine polymer chains.

cards.title: Reflecting light at Brewster's angle so only one polarisation bounces
cards.meaning: Brewster's law gives the special incidence angle θ_p where the electric field vibrating in the plane of incidence has zero reflection.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="20" y="96" width="220" height="64" class="s ok"/><line x1="130" y1="18" x2="130" y2="164" class="gk"/><line x1="46" y1="32" x2="130" y2="96" class="lk"/><line x1="130" y1="96" x2="214" y2="32" class="lk"/><line x1="130" y1="96" x2="178" y2="158" class="ik"/><circle cx="158" cy="75" r="3" class="f"/><circle cx="182" cy="56" r="3" class="f"/><circle cx="202" cy="41" r="3" class="f"/><text x="34" y="84" class="t">n₁</text><text x="34" y="118" class="t">n₂</text><text x="114" y="56" class="t">θ_p</text><text x="144" y="56" class="t">θ_p</text><text x="142" y="138" class="t">θ_r</text><text x="206" y="76" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Reflected (s-polarised)</text><text x="190" y="114" class="t">90°</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the interface at Brewster's angle θ_p: the reflected ray (dots, perpendicular to the page) and refracted ray are 90° apart.
cards.example: Sunlight reflecting off water (n₂ = 1.33) near θ_p ≈ 53° is horizontally polarised glare, which vertically polarised sunglasses block.
cards.bridge: Combining Brewster's law tan θ_p = n₂/n₁ with Snell's law n₁ sin θ_p = n₂ sin θ_r proves that cos θ_p = sin θ_r, so θ_p + θ_r = 90°.

cards.label: 02 · §22.3.2 Definition
cards.title: What is Brewster's law?
cards.body: Brewster's law states that when unpolarised light hits an interface at θ_p = tan⁻¹(n₂/n₁), the reflected ray is linearly polarised perpendicular to the plane of incidence and is 90° to the refracted ray.

cards.label: 03 · §22.3.2 Derivation
cards.title: Brewster's law and right angle between reflected and refracted rays
cards.legend: Dielectric interface between \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) with polarising angle \(\theta_p\) and refraction angle \(\theta_r\) (Eq. 22.10, Fig. 22.9).

phases.name: Brewster's law
phases.why: write tan θ_p = n₂ / n₁ as sin θ_p / cos θ_p

phases.name: Snell's law
phases.why: equate the Brewster ratio to Snell's law sin θ_p / sin θ_r

phases.name: Equate cosines
phases.why: cancel sin θ_p and take reciprocals to get sin θ_r = cos θ_p

phases.name: Right angle
phases.why: replace cos θ_p by sin(90° - θ_p) to show θ_p + θ_r = 90°

steps.note: Start from Brewster's law at the polarising angle \(\theta_p\) (Eq. 22.10).
Rewrite \(\tan\theta_p\) as \(\sin\theta_p / \cos\theta_p\).

ask.q: By Snell's law at angle \(\theta_p\), what else equals \(n_2 / n_1\)?
ask.why: Snell's law \(n_1\sin\theta_p = n_2\sin\theta_r\) gives \(n_2/n_1 = \sin\theta_p/\sin\theta_r\).

move.label: Write Snell's law at incidence angle θ_p

steps.note: Write Snell's law of refraction for the transmitted ray at angle \(\theta_r\).
Equate the two expressions for \(n_2 / n_1\).

ask.q: Which move cancels \(\sin\theta_p\) from the numerators?
ask.why: Since \(\sin\theta_p \neq 0\), dividing both sides by \(\sin\theta_p\) leaves \(1/\sin\theta_r = 1/\cos\theta_p\).

steps.note: Divide both sides by \(\sin\theta_p\).
Take the reciprocal of both sides.

ask.q: Which cofunction identity rewrites \(\cos\theta_p\) as a sine?
ask.why: For complementary angles, \(\cos\theta_p = \sin(90^\circ - \theta_p)\).

steps.note: Replace \(\cos\theta_p\) with \(\sin(90^\circ - \theta_p)\).

ask.q: Since \(\theta_r = 90^\circ - \theta_p\), what is the angle between the reflected and refracted rays?
ask.why: Along the normal, \(180^\circ - (\theta_p + \theta_r) = 180^\circ - 90^\circ = 90^\circ\) (§22.3.2).

move.label: Equate acute angles and add θ_p to both sides

steps.note: At Brewster's angle, the reflected and transmitted rays are at right angles (§22.3.2).

cards.title: Eliminating one of the two crystal beams by absorption or reflection
cards.meaning: When a crystal splits light into two polarised beams, we obtain one clean polarised beam either by absorbing one beam (dichroism) or reflecting it aside (Nicol prism).
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="24" width="96" height="132" rx="10" class="s ok"/><polygon points="140,136 160,44 238,44 218,136" class="s ok"/><line x1="140" y1="136" x2="238" y2="44" class="gk"/><line x1="18" y1="90" x2="102" y2="72" class="lk"/><line x1="18" y1="90" x2="64" y2="114" class="ik"/><line x1="124" y1="96" x2="188" y2="80" class="lk"/><line x1="188" y1="80" x2="248" y2="80" class="lk"/><line x1="124" y1="96" x2="180" y2="98" class="ik"/><line x1="180" y1="98" x2="196" y2="144" class="ik"/><text x="62" y="42" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Tourmaline</text><text x="62" y="146" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Dichroism</text><text x="190" y="32" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Nicol prism (Canada balsam)</text><text x="232" y="70" text-anchor="middle" class="t">e-ray</text><text x="204" y="158" text-anchor="middle" class="t">o-ray (TIR)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Compare tourmaline on the left (absorbs one beam by dichroism) with the Nicol prism on the right (Canada balsam layer reflects the o-ray by total internal reflection).
cards.example: In a Nicol prism, Canada balsam has a refractive index between n_o and n_e, so it acts as a rarer medium for the o-ray and reflects it away.
cards.bridge: A fourth method is scattering (§22.3.4): unpolarised light scattered at 90° by gas molecules is linearly polarised because light waves are transverse.

cards.label: 04 · §§22.3.3–22.3.4 Definition
cards.title: What are dichroism, a Nicol prism, and scattering polarisation?
cards.body: Dichroism is selective absorption of one polarised beam (as in tourmaline). A Nicol prism uses Canada balsam to remove the ordinary ray by total internal reflection. Gas scattering at 90° is also linearly polarised.

cards.label: 05 · §22.3.2 Worked example
cards.title: Brewster angle for air-water interface and polarised sunglasses (§22.3.2)
cards.body: For sunlight hitting water (\(n_1 \approx 1, n_2 \approx 1.33\)) near \(\theta_p \approx 53^\circ\), the reflected glare is horizontally polarised (perpendicular to the vertical plane of incidence). Polarised sunglasses have a vertical pass axis to block this horizontal glare.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In a wire-grid polariser with wires along \(y\), which electric component passes through?
cards.why: Currents along the \(y\)-wires absorb \(E_y\) by Joule heating, while \(E_x\) perpendicular to the wires passes through (§22.3.1).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: At Brewster's angle \(\theta_p\), what is the angle between the reflected and transmitted rays?
cards.why: Since \(\tan\theta_p = n_2/n_1 = \sin\theta_p/\sin\theta_r\), \(\cos\theta_p = \sin\theta_r\), so the reflected and transmitted rays are at \(90^\circ\) (§22.3.2).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: Selective absorption of one polarised beam in a crystal like tourmaline is called ______.
cards.why: The property of selectively absorbing one of the two doubly refracted polarised beams is called dichroism (§22.3.3).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: Light in air (\(n_1 = 1\)) hits glass of index \(n_2 = \sqrt{3}\) at Brewster's angle. Find \(\theta_p\) in degrees.
cards.why: From \(\tan\theta_p = n_2/n_1 = \sqrt{3}\), \(\theta_p = \tan^{-1}(\sqrt{3}) = 60^\circ\).

sheets.title: Polariser, analyser & Malus's law
sheets.source: Unit 19 · Ghatak ch. 22 §22.2 (PDF pp. 358–360; Book 2 not available); syllabus item 19

cards.title: Resolving the electric field along a tilted analyser
cards.meaning: When a linearly polarised wave of amplitude E₀ hits a second Polaroid tilted at angle θ, only the component E₀ cos θ parallel to the new pass axis gets through.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="130" cy="94" r="62" class="s ok"/><line x1="56" y1="94" x2="204" y2="94" class="gk"/><line x1="130" y1="24" x2="130" y2="164" class="lk"/><line x1="130" y1="94" x2="178" y2="46" class="ik"/><line x1="130" y1="36" x2="168" y2="56" class="gk"/><path d="M 130 62 A 32 32 0 0 1 152 71" class="lk"/><circle cx="130" cy="36" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="168" cy="56" r="4" class="f"/><text x="116" y="38" text-anchor="end" class="t">E₀ (from P₁)</text><text x="142" y="56" class="t">θ</text><text x="184" y="52" class="t">P₂ pass axis</text><text x="184" y="72" class="t">E₀ cos θ</text><text x="130" y="174" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Intensity I ∝ (E₀ cos θ)² → I = I₀ cos²θ</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at vertical amplitude E₀ from P₁ projected onto the tilted pass axis of analyser P₂ to give transmitted amplitude E₀ cos θ.
cards.example: At θ = 60°, cos 60° = 1/2 so the electric field amplitude drops to E₀/2 and the intensity drops to (1/2)² I₀ = I₀/4.
cards.bridge: Because light intensity is proportional to the square of electric field amplitude, squaring E₀ cos θ gives Malus's law I = I₀ cos²θ.

cards.label: 01 · §22.2 Definition
cards.title: What is Malus's law?
cards.body: In Malus's law, a linearly polarised beam of intensity I₀ hits an analyser tilted at angle θ to the electric field. The transmitted intensity is I = I₀ cos²θ.

cards.label: 02 · §22.2 Derivation
cards.title: Malus's law for intensity transmitted by an analyser
cards.legend: Incident linearly polarised wave of amplitude \(E_0\) along \(x\) (intensity \(I_0 = K E_0^2\)) incident on analyser \(P_2\) at angle \(\theta\) (Eq. 22.9, Fig. 22.6).

phases.name: Resolve field
phases.why: resolve incident amplitude E₀ along and perpendicular to P₂'s pass axis

phases.name: Square amplitude
phases.why: square the transmitted electric field component E_∥

phases.name: Intensity ratio
phases.why: multiply by proportionality constant K so I = K E_∥²

phases.name: Malus's law
phases.why: substitute I₀ = K E₀² to obtain I = I₀ cos²θ

steps.note: Resolve the incident electric field \(E_0\) along the pass axis of analyser \(P_2\) at angle \(\theta\).

move.label: Write perpendicular component absorbed by analyser P₂

steps.note: The perpendicular component \(E_0\sin\theta\) is absorbed by \(P_2\), so only \(E_\parallel\) emerges.

ask.q: Which component of \(E_0\) is transmitted by the analyser \(P_2\)?
ask.why: The analyser transmits only the component \(E_0\cos\theta\) parallel to its pass axis (§22.2).

move.label: Square both sides of E_∥ = E₀ cos θ

steps.note: Square the emergent amplitude \(E_\parallel\) since intensity is proportional to amplitude squared.

ask.q: How is wave intensity \(I\) related to the emergent amplitude \(E_\parallel\)?
ask.why: The intensity of an electromagnetic wave is proportional to the square of its electric field amplitude.

steps.note: Multiply both sides by the intensity proportionality constant \(K\).
Replace \(K E_\parallel^2\) on the left with emergent intensity \(I\).

ask.q: What does \(K E_0^2\) represent when the two Polaroids are parallel (\(\theta = 0\))?
ask.why: When \(\theta = 0\), \(\cos\theta = 1\) and the emergent intensity is \(I_0 = K E_0^2\) (§22.2).

steps.note: Substitute \(I_0 = K E_0^2\) to obtain Malus's law (Eq. 22.9).

ask.q: According to Malus's law, what is \(I\) when \(\theta = 90^\circ\)?
ask.why: Since \(\cos 90^\circ = 0\), \(I = I_0\cos^2 90^\circ = 0\) (complete extinction).

cards.title: Parallel, 45-degree, and crossed Polaroids
cards.meaning: Crossed polarisers have their pass axes at 90° to each other, so the second sheet blocks all light transmitted by the first.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="34" width="70" height="96" rx="8" class="s ok"/><rect x="95" y="34" width="70" height="96" rx="8" class="s ok"/><rect x="176" y="34" width="70" height="96" rx="8" class="s ok"/><line x1="49" y1="48" x2="49" y2="116" class="lk"/><line x1="110" y1="104" x2="150" y2="60" class="lk"/><line x1="211" y1="48" x2="211" y2="116" class="gk"/><line x1="188" y1="82" x2="234" y2="82" class="ik"/><circle cx="211" cy="82" r="6" class="f"/><text x="49" y="26" text-anchor="middle" class="t">(a) θ = 0°</text><text x="49" y="148" text-anchor="middle" class="t">I = I₀ (100%)</text><text x="130" y="26" text-anchor="middle" class="t">(b) θ = 45°</text><text x="130" y="148" text-anchor="middle" class="t">I = I₀/2 (50%)</text><text x="211" y="26" text-anchor="middle" class="t">(c) θ = 90°</text><text x="211" y="148" text-anchor="middle" class="t">I = 0 (Dark)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Compare Fig. 22.7(a) parallel (full I₀), Fig. 22.7(b) at 45° (half intensity I₀/2), and Fig. 22.7(c) crossed at 90° (zero intensity).
cards.example: As you rotate P₂ through one full turn (0° to 360°), you see two bright maxima (0° and 180°) and two dark extinctions (90° and 270°).
cards.bridge: Either P₁ or P₂ can be rotated to produce the exact same cos²θ variation in transmitted intensity.

cards.label: 03 · §22.2 Definition
cards.title: What are crossed polarisers and how does rotation change intensity?
cards.body: Crossed polarisers have perpendicular pass axes (θ = 90°), giving zero transmitted intensity. Rotating one Polaroid through 360° produces two maxima (0°, 180°) and two zero minima (90°, 270°).

cards.label: 04 · §22.2 Intensity graph
cards.title: Malus's law intensity curve I = I₀ cos²θ
cards.body: As analyser angle θ varies from 0 to 2π, transmitted intensity I = I₀ cos²θ reaches maxima I₀ at θ = 0, π, 2π, equals 0.5 I₀ at θ = π/4, and drops to zero at θ = π/2 and 3π/2.

cards.label: 05 · §22.2 Worked example
cards.title: Transmitted intensity at θ = 45°, 60°, and 90° (§22.2)
cards.body: When two Polaroids are oriented at \(45^\circ\), \(\cos^2 45^\circ = 1/2\) so \(50\%\) of the linearly polarised intensity \(I_0\) passes through. At \(60^\circ\), \(25\%\) passes through, and at \(90^\circ\) no light passes through.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: How many times does intensity become zero when an analyser rotates through \(360^\circ\)?
cards.why: Since \(I = I_0\cos^2\theta\), complete extinction occurs twice per revolution at \(\theta = 90^\circ\) and \(\theta = 270^\circ\) (§22.2).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: When two Polaroids are oriented at \(45^\circ\), what fraction of \(I_0\) passes the second?

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: Two Polaroids with their pass axes at \(90^\circ\) to each other are said to be ______.
cards.why: When two Polaroids have mutually perpendicular pass axes (\(\theta = 90^\circ\)), they are crossed and block all light (§22.2).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: Polarised light of intensity \(100\text{ W/m}^2\) hits an analyser at \(\theta = 60^\circ\). Find emergent intensity in \(\text{W/m}^2\).
cards.why: From Malus's law, \(I = 100\cos^2 60^\circ = 100 \times (0.5)^2 = 25\text{ W/m}^2\).

sheets.title: Double refraction & Huygens
sheets.source: Unit 20 · Ghatak ch. 22 §22.5 (PDF pp. 365–368; Book 2 not available); syllabus item 20

cards.title: Why a calcite crystal shows a double image of a printed line
cards.meaning: Double refraction happens when an unpolarised beam enters an anisotropic crystal like calcite and splits into an ordinary ray (o-ray) and an extraordinary ray (e-ray).
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="84" y="34" width="84" height="112" class="s ok"/><line x1="18" y1="106" x2="84" y2="106" class="lk"/><line x1="84" y1="106" x2="226" y2="106" class="ik"/><line x1="84" y1="106" x2="168" y2="62" class="lk"/><line x1="168" y1="62" x2="226" y2="62" class="lk"/><line x1="96" y1="86" x2="156" y2="54" class="gk"/><circle cx="184" cy="106" r="3" class="f"/><circle cx="204" cy="106" r="3" class="f"/><line x1="184" y1="52" x2="184" y2="72" class="lk"/><line x1="204" y1="52" x2="204" y2="72" class="lk"/><text x="126" y="26" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Calcite crystal</text><text x="126" y="134" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Optic axis (dashed)</text><text x="212" y="44" text-anchor="middle" class="t">e-ray (∥ plane)</text><text x="212" y="128" text-anchor="middle" class="t">o-ray (⊥ page)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the unpolarised beam entering calcite (Fig. 22.20): the o-ray goes straight with dot vibrations, while the e-ray bends aside with bar vibrations.
cards.example: When you rotate the calcite crystal about the normal NN', the ordinary image stays fixed while the extraordinary image revolves around it!
cards.bridge: The o-ray always obeys Snell's law with D ⊥ optic axis (Eq. 22.43), while the e-ray has D in the plane containing k and the optic axis (Eq. 22.44).

cards.label: 01 · §22.5 Definition
cards.title: What are double refraction, the ordinary ray, and the extraordinary ray?
cards.body: Double refraction splits light in an anisotropic crystal into two linearly polarised rays. The ordinary ray (o-ray) obeys Snell's law (D ⊥ optic axis), while the extraordinary ray (e-ray) has D in the optic-axis plane.

cards.title: Sphere and ellipsoid wavelets in negative and positive crystals
cards.meaning: The optic axis is the special direction in a uniaxial crystal along which the ordinary sphere and extraordinary ellipsoid touch because both rays have speed c/n_o.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="70" cy="90" r="32" class="ik"/><ellipse cx="70" cy="90" rx="32" ry="48" class="lk"/><line x1="24" y1="90" x2="116" y2="90" class="gk"/><circle cx="190" cy="90" r="46" class="ik"/><ellipse cx="190" cy="90" rx="46" ry="30" class="lk"/><line x1="136" y1="90" x2="244" y2="90" class="gk"/><text x="70" y="24" text-anchor="middle" class="t">(a) Negative (n_e < n_o)</text><text x="70" y="156" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Calcite: v_re(π/2) > v_ro</text><text x="190" y="24" text-anchor="middle" class="t">(b) Positive (n_e > n_o)</text><text x="190" y="156" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Quartz: v_re(π/2) < v_ro</text></svg>
cards.picture: Compare Fig. 22.22(a) negative crystal (e-ray ellipsoid outside o-ray sphere) with Fig. 22.22(b) positive crystal (e-ray ellipsoid inside o-ray sphere).
cards.example: Along the horizontal optic axis (θ = 0), the sphere and ellipsoid touch at radius c/n_o; perpendicular to it (θ = π/2), the e-ray speed is c/n_e.
cards.bridge: Using Huygens' secondary wavelets with these spherical and ellipsoidal velocity surfaces explains double refraction at any angle of incidence.

cards.label: 02 · §22.5 Definition
cards.title: What are the optic axis, negative crystals, and positive crystals?
cards.body: The optic axis is the direction in a uniaxial crystal where o-ray and e-ray speeds equal c/n_o. In negative crystals (calcite, n_e < n_o) the e-ellipsoid lies outside the o-sphere; in positive (n_e > n_o) inside.

cards.label: 03 · §22.5 Derivation
cards.title: Extraordinary ray velocity surface and refractive index
cards.legend: Extraordinary ray velocity \(v_{re}(\theta)\) at angle \(\theta\) to the optic axis (\(z\)-axis), semi-axes \(a = c/n_o\) and \(b = c/n_e\), and ray refractive index \(n_{re} = c/v_{re}\) (Eqs. 22.37–22.45).

phases.name: Velocity law
phases.why: start from the extraordinary ray velocity equation at angle θ

phases.name: Polar ellipse
phases.why: set a = c/n_o, b = c/n_e, ρ = v_{re} and convert to Cartesian (z, x)

phases.name: Ray index
phases.why: multiply Eq. (22.37) by c² and substitute n_{re} = c / v_{re}

phases.name: Result
phases.why: take the square root to obtain the extraordinary ray refractive index

steps.note: Start from the extraordinary ray velocity equation at angle \(\theta\) to the optic axis (Eq. 22.37).
Set semi-axes \(a = c/n_o\), \(b = c/n_e\), and polar radius \(\rho = v_{re}\) (Eq. 22.39).

ask.q: Along the optic axis (\(\theta = 0\)), what does \(v_{re}\) equal?
ask.why: At \(\theta = 0\), \(\sin\theta = 0\) and \(\cos\theta = 1\), so \(v_{re} = c/n_o = v_{ro}\) (§22.5).

steps.note: Multiply both sides by \(\rho^2\).

ask.q: In polar coordinates \((\rho, \theta)\) around the \(z\)-axis, what are \(z\) and \(x\)?
ask.why: With \(\theta\) measured from the \(z\)-axis, \(z = \rho\cos\theta\) and \(x = \rho\sin\theta\) (§22.5).

steps.note: Thus plotting \(v_{re}(\theta)\) in 3D gives an ellipsoid of revolution (Eq. 22.38).

move.label: Multiply Eq. (22.37) by c²

steps.note: Multiply both sides of Eq. (22.37) by \(c^2\) to express \((c/v_{re})^2\).

ask.q: How is the extraordinary ray refractive index \(n_{re}\) defined?
ask.why: By definition (Eq. 22.45), the ray refractive index is \(n_{re} = c / v_{re}\).

steps.note: Substitute \(n_{re} = c / v_{re}\) on the left-hand side.

ask.q: Perpendicular to the optic axis (\(\theta = \pi/2\)), what does \(n_{re}\) equal?
ask.why: At \(\theta = \pi/2\), \(\cos\theta = 0\) and \(\sin\theta = 1\), so \(n_{re} = n_e\).

steps.note: Take the positive square root to get the extraordinary ray refractive index (Eq. 22.45).

cards.label: 04 · §§22.5.1–22.5.2 Huygens
cards.title: Huygens' construction for normal and oblique incidence (Figs. 22.23–22.25)
cards.body: Huygens' construction draws spheres of radius c/n_o (tangent OO' → o-ray BO) and ellipsoids of axes c/n_o, c/n_e (tangent EE' → e-ray BE). If the optic axis is parallel to the surface, both travel along BO.
examples: Axis ⊥ incidence: sin i/sin r = n_e

cards.label: 05 · §22.5 Worked comparison
cards.title: Negative vs positive uniaxial crystals perpendicular to the optic axis
cards.body: Perpendicular to the optic axis (\(\theta = \pi/2\)), the e-wave travels faster than the o-wave in a negative crystal like calcite (\(n_e = 1.486 < n_o = 1.658\)), and slower than the o-wave in a positive crystal like quartz (\(n_e = 1.553 > n_o = 1.544\)).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In a negative uniaxial crystal like calcite, how do \(n_e\) and \(n_o\) compare?
cards.why: In a negative crystal like calcite, \(n_e < n_o\), so perpendicular to the optic axis \(v_{re} = c/n_e > c/n_o = v_{ro}\) (Eq. 22.40).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: When light hits a crystal normally with the optic axis parallel to the surface:
options: The two rays split apart in angle
Both rays travel together at different speeds
Both rays travel at the same speed
cards.why: In Fig. 22.24(a,b), when the optic axis is parallel to the surface, both waves travel along the normal with different speeds \(c/n_o\) and \(c/n_e\) (§22.5.1).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: Crystals like calcite and quartz that have only one optic axis are called ______ crystals.
cards.why: Crystals with a single direction along which the two rays have the same speed are called uniaxial crystals (§22.5).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: Along the optic axis (\(\theta = 0^\circ\)), if \(n_o = 1.658\) and \(n_e = 1.486\), find \(n_{re}\).
cards.why: At \(\theta = 0^\circ\), \(n_{re} = \sqrt{n_o^2\cos^2 0^\circ + n_e^2\sin^2 0^\circ} = n_o = 1.658\) (Eq. 22.45).

sheets.title: Quarter-wave & half-wave plates
sheets.source: Unit 21 · Ghatak ch. 22 §22.6 (PDF pp. 369–371; Book 2 not available); syllabus item 21

cards.title: Turning linear polarisation into a circle with a crystal plate
cards.meaning: A quarter-wave plate is a crystal slice cut parallel to its optic axis that delays one component by a quarter of a wavelength (phase π/2) behind the other.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="18" y1="90" x2="242" y2="90" class="gk"/><line x1="34" y1="122" x2="74" y2="58" class="lk"/><rect x="98" y="30" width="54" height="120" rx="6" class="s ok"/><line x1="112" y1="30" x2="112" y2="150" class="gk"/><line x1="125" y1="30" x2="125" y2="150" class="gk"/><line x1="138" y1="30" x2="138" y2="150" class="gk"/><circle cx="198" cy="90" r="32" class="lk"/><line x1="198" y1="90" x2="221" y2="67" class="ik"/><circle cx="221" cy="67" r="4" class="f"/><text x="54" y="46" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Linear (φ = 45°)</text><text x="125" y="22" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Calcite QWP (θ = π/2)</text><text x="125" y="166" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Optic axis ∥ surface</text><text x="198" y="46" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Circular (LCP)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at Fig. 22.26: linearly polarised light at φ = 45° enters a calcite QWP (optic axis parallel to surface) and emerges circularly polarised.
cards.example: Because φ = 45°, the o-wave (along x) and e-wave (along y) have equal amplitudes E₀/√2; a π/2 phase shift turns them into sin ωt and cos ωt.
cards.bridge: For a phase shift θ = (2m + 1)π/2, the required plate thickness is d = (2m + 1)λ₀ / [4(n_o - n_e)].

cards.label: 01 · §22.6 Definition
cards.title: What is a quarter-wave plate (QWP)?
cards.body: A quarter-wave plate is a uniaxial crystal plate cut with its optic axis parallel to the surface. Its thickness d creates a π/2 phase difference (λ₀/4 path difference) between o- and e-waves.

cards.label: 02 · §22.6 Derivation
cards.title: Phase difference and thickness of a quarter-wave plate
cards.legend: Negative uniaxial crystal plate of thickness \(d\) with optic axis along \(y\), ordinary index \(n_o\), extraordinary index \(n_e\), and free-space wavenumber \(k = 2\pi / \lambda_0\) (Eqs. 22.50–22.53).

phases.name: Wave phases
phases.why: write the phases θ_o and θ_e accumulated across thickness d

phases.name: Phase lag
phases.why: subtract θ_e from θ_o and substitute k = 2π / λ₀

phases.name: Quarter wave
phases.why: set phase difference θ equal to an odd multiple (2m + 1)π/2

phases.name: Plate thickness
phases.why: solve for the QWP thickness d

steps.note: Inside a crystal of thickness \(d\), the \(x\)-component travels as an o-wave with phase \(\theta_o = n_o k d\).

move.label: Write phase of extraordinary wave at emerging surface

steps.note: The \(y\)-component (along the optic axis) travels as an e-wave with phase \(\theta_e = n_e k d\).

ask.q: How do we find the phase difference \(\theta\) between the o- and e-waves at \(z = d\)?
ask.why: The relative phase difference introduced by the crystal plate is \(\theta = \theta_o - \theta_e\) (Eq. 22.50).

steps.tex: \theta_o - \theta_e = n_o k d - n_e k d
steps.note: Subtract \(\theta_e\) from \(\theta_o\).
Set \(\theta = \theta_o - \theta_e\) and factor out \(kd\) (Eq. 22.50).

ask.q: How is the free-space wavenumber \(k\) related to wavelength \(\lambda_0\)?
ask.why: In free space, \(k = \omega / c = 2\pi / \lambda_0\).

steps.note: Replace \(k\) with \(2\pi / \lambda_0\) to relate phase difference \(\theta\) to path difference \((n_o - n_e)d\).

ask.q: For a quarter-wave plate (QWP), what phase difference \(\theta\) is required?
ask.why: A quarter-wave plate introduces an odd multiple of \(\pi/2\), i.e., \(\theta = (2m + 1)\pi/2\) (Eq. 22.53).

steps.note: Set \(\theta = (2m + 1)\pi/2\) for a general quarter-wave plate (Eq. 22.53).
Multiply both sides by \(\lambda_0 / [2\pi(n_o - n_e)]\); the factor \(\pi\) cancels.

ask.q: For \(m = 0\), what is the minimum thickness \(d\) of a calcite QWP?
ask.why: Setting \(m = 0\) in Eq. (22.53) gives the minimum QWP thickness \(d = \lambda_0 / [4(n_o - n_e)]\) (Eq. 22.52).

steps.note: Swap sides to obtain the quarter-wave plate thickness formula (Eq. 22.53).

cards.title: Flipping one electric component to rotate a plane wave by 90°
cards.meaning: A half-wave plate delays one component by half a wavelength (phase π), which reverses its sign and flips the polarisation across the optic axis.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="18" y1="90" x2="242" y2="90" class="gk"/><line x1="34" y1="124" x2="74" y2="56" class="lk"/><rect x="98" y="30" width="58" height="120" rx="6" class="s ok"/><line x1="114" y1="30" x2="114" y2="150" class="gk"/><line x1="127" y1="30" x2="127" y2="150" class="gk"/><line x1="140" y1="30" x2="140" y2="150" class="gk"/><line x1="182" y1="56" x2="222" y2="124" class="ik"/><text x="54" y="44" text-anchor="middle" class="t">In: +45° to y</text><text x="127" y="22" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Calcite HWP (θ = π)</text><text x="127" y="166" text-anchor="middle" class="t">E_x → -E_x, E_y → +E_y</text><text x="202" y="44" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Out: 135° (rot 90°)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at Fig. 22.27: a linearly polarised wave at +45° to the y-axis has E_x reversed by the HWP, rotating the polarisation by 90° to 135°.
cards.example: Because cos(ωt - π) = -cos ωt, the x-component flips sign while the y-component stays +cos ωt.
cards.bridge: Similarly, a HWP turns left-circularly polarised light (LCP) into right-circularly polarised light (RCP), and vice versa.

cards.label: 03 · §22.6 Definition
cards.title: What is a half-wave plate (HWP)?
cards.body: A half-wave plate is a crystal plate with optic axis parallel to the surface that introduces a phase difference of π (path difference λ₀/2). It rotates linear polarisation at angle φ by 2φ and flips LCP to RCP.
cards.tex: d = (2m + 1)\frac{\lambda_0}{2|n_o - n_e|}, \quad E_x = -\frac{E_0}{\sqrt{2}}\cos\omega t, \quad E_y = \frac{E_0}{\sqrt{2}}\cos\omega t

cards.label: 04 · §22.6 Examples 22.6–22.8
cards.title: Worked example: calcite QWP thickness and emergent states
cards.body: For calcite at \(\lambda_0 = 5893\text{ \AA}\) (\(n_o = 1.65836, n_e = 1.48641\)), minimum QWP thickness is \(0.000857\text{ mm}\) (Example 22.6). A calcite crystal of thickness \(0.005141\text{ mm}\) gives \(\theta = 3\pi\), acting as a HWP that converts LCP into RCP (Example 22.7).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Linearly polarised light at \(45^\circ\) to the optic axis passes through a QWP. It emerges:
cards.why: At \(\phi = 45^\circ\), the two orthogonal components have equal amplitudes and a \(\pi/2\) phase shift, producing circularly polarised light (Eq. 22.51).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What does a half-wave plate (HWP) do to left-circularly polarised (LCP) light?
cards.why: A phase shift of \(\pi\) reverses one component (\(\sin(\omega t - \pi) = -\sin\omega t\)), converting LCP into RCP (Example 22.7).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: If phase difference \(\theta\) is not a multiple of \(\pi/2\), the emergent beam is ______ polarised.
cards.why: When \(\theta \neq \pi/2, \pi, 3\pi/2, 2\pi, \dots\), the superposition of the o- and e-waves is elliptically polarised (§22.6).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: For \(\lambda_0 = 600\text{ nm}\) and \(|n_o - n_e| = 0.15\), find minimum QWP thickness \(d\) in \(\mu\text{m}\).
cards.why: \(d = \frac{\lambda_0}{4|n_o - n_e|} = \frac{0.6\,\mu\text{m}}{4 \times 0.15} = \frac{0.6}{0.6} = 1\,\mu\text{m}\).

sheets.title: Analysis & optical activity
sheets.source: Unit 22 · Ghatak ch. 22 §§22.7–22.8 (PDF pp. 372–375; Book 2 not available); syllabus item 22

cards.title: Telling all seven states of polarisation apart with a Polaroid and QWP
cards.meaning: To the human eye all polarisations look the same, so we first rotate a single Polaroid and then insert a quarter-wave plate if needed.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="12" y="14" width="72" height="152" rx="8" class="s ok"/><rect x="94" y="14" width="72" height="152" rx="8" class="s ok"/><rect x="176" y="14" width="72" height="152" rx="8" class="s ok"/><text x="48" y="34" text-anchor="middle" class="t">(i) Zero min</text><text x="48" y="76" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Polaroid</text><text x="48" y="94" text-anchor="middle" class="t">alone gives</text><text x="48" y="112" text-anchor="middle" class="t">2 dark zeros</text><text x="48" y="148" text-anchor="middle" class="t">→ Linear</text><text x="130" y="34" text-anchor="middle" class="t">(ii) Constant</text><text x="130" y="68" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Add QWP:</text><text x="130" y="92" text-anchor="middle" class="t">0 min → Circ</text><text x="130" y="114" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Const → Unpol</text><text x="130" y="136" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Var → Mix</text><text x="212" y="34" text-anchor="middle" class="t">(iii) Varies</text><text x="212" y="68" text-anchor="middle" class="t">QWP ∥ I_max:</text><text x="212" y="92" text-anchor="middle" class="t">0 min → Ellip</text><text x="212" y="114" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Same → Lin+U</text><text x="212" y="136" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Shift → Ell+U</text></svg>
cards.picture: Compare the three outcomes of rotating a Polaroid (§22.7): (i) two zero minima → linear; (ii) constant → test with QWP; (iii) varies without zero → align QWP with I_max.
cards.example: Circularly polarised light and unpolarised light both give constant intensity through a rotating Polaroid, but a QWP turns circular light into linear light (giving two zero minima)!
cards.bridge: Similarly, aligning a QWP with the maximum-intensity axis turns pure elliptically polarised light into linearly polarised light.

cards.label: 01 · §22.7 Definition
cards.title: What is the procedure for analysis of polarised light?
cards.body: Rotating a Polaroid gives extinction for linear light, constant intensity for unpolarised or circular light, and partial variation for elliptical or mixed light. Adding a QWP distinguishes circular and elliptical states.

cards.title: Why sugar solution and quartz twist the plane of polarisation
cards.meaning: Optical activity is the steady rotation of the plane of linear polarisation because the medium's left-circular (LCP) and right-circular (RCP) modes travel at slightly different speeds.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="48" cy="88" r="28" class="lk"/><circle cx="124" cy="88" r="28" class="ik"/><line x1="48" y1="88" x2="34" y2="64" class="lk"/><line x1="124" y1="88" x2="148" y2="74" class="ik"/><line x1="210" y1="34" x2="210" y2="142" class="gk"/><line x1="176" y1="88" x2="244" y2="88" class="gk"/><line x1="188" y1="126" x2="232" y2="50" class="lk"/><path d="M 210 56 A 32 32 0 0 1 226 60" class="lk"/><text x="48" y="38" text-anchor="middle" class="t">RCP (φ₁ = k_R z)</text><text x="86" y="92" text-anchor="middle" class="t">+</text><text x="124" y="38" text-anchor="middle" class="t">LCP (φ₂ = k_L z)</text><text x="164" y="92" text-anchor="middle" class="t">=</text><text x="210" y="24" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Rotated LP (φ)</text><text x="130" y="164" text-anchor="middle" class="t">φ(z) = ½(k_L - k_R)z = (π/λ)(n_L - n_R)z</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at Fig. 22.28: adding RCP (rotated by φ₁ = k_R z) and LCP (rotated by φ₂ = k_L z) produces a linearly polarised wave rotated by φ = ½(φ₂ - φ₁).
cards.example: In a sugar solution, the rotation angle φ is proportional to both tube length z and sugar concentration, which industry uses to measure sugar content.
cards.bridge: If n_L > n_R (φ > 0), the medium is right-handed (dextro-rotatory); if n_L < n_R (φ < 0), it is left-handed (laevo-rotatory).

cards.label: 02 · §22.8 Definition
cards.title: What is optical activity?
cards.body: Optical activity is the rotation of the plane of polarisation by φ(z) = (π/λ)(n_L - n_R)z because LCP and RCP modes have different indices n_L and n_R. Dextro-rotatory media have n_L > n_R; laevo-rotatory have n_L < n_R.

cards.label: 03 · §22.8 Derivation
cards.title: Rotation of plane of polarisation in an optically active medium
cards.legend: Superposition of RCP wave (\(k_R = \frac{\omega}{c}n_R\)) and LCP wave (\(k_L = \frac{\omega}{c}n_L\)) propagating along \(+z\), with \(\theta(z) = \frac{1}{2}(k_L + k_R)z\) (Eqs. 22.56–22.58, Fig. 22.28).

phases.name: Superpose x
phases.why: add the x-components of the RCP and LCP waves

phases.name: Superpose y
phases.why: add the y-components of the RCP and LCP waves

phases.name: Rotation angle
phases.why: divide E_y by E_x to find the rotation angle φ(z)

phases.name: Refractive indices
phases.why: substitute k_L = 2πn_L/λ and k_R = 2πn_R/λ

steps.tex: E_x = E_0[\cos(k_R z - \omega t) + \cos(k_L z - \omega t)]
steps.note: Add the \(x\)-components of the RCP wave (Eq. 22.56) and LCP wave (Eq. 22.57).
Combine the two cosines, where \(\theta(z) = \frac{1}{2}(k_L + k_R)z\).

ask.q: At \(z = 0\), what are \(E_x\) and \(E_y\) when the RCP and LCP waves add?
ask.why: At \(z = 0\), the \(y\)-components \(-\sin(-\omega t)\) and \(+\sin(-\omega t)\) cancel, leaving linear polarisation along \(x\).

move.label: Add y-components of RCP and LCP waves (Eqs. 22.56–22.57)

steps.tex: E_y = E_0[-\sin(k_R z - \omega t) + \sin(k_L z - \omega t)]
steps.note: Add the \(y\)-components \(E_y^R\) and \(E_y^L\) after propagating distance \(z\).
Both \(E_x\) and \(E_y\) oscillate in phase as \(\cos[\omega t - \theta(z)]\), so the wave stays linearly polarised.

ask.q: Since \(E_x\) and \(E_y\) oscillate in phase, how is the rotation angle \(\phi(z)\) found?
ask.why: For a vector with components \((E_x, E_y)\), the angle \(\phi(z)\) with the \(x\)-axis satisfies \(\tan\phi(z) = E_y / E_x\).

move.label: Divide E_y by E_x to get tan φ(z)

steps.note: Dividing \(E_y\) by \(E_x\) cancels \(2E_0\cos[\omega t - \theta(z)]\).
Equate the angles inside the tangent.

ask.q: What replaces \(k_L - k_R\) in terms of free-space wavelength \(\lambda\)?
ask.why: Since \(k_L = (2\pi/\lambda)n_L\) and \(k_R = (2\pi/\lambda)n_R\), \(k_L - k_R = (2\pi/\lambda)(n_L - n_R)\).

steps.note: This gives the angle of optical rotation after distance \(z\) (Eq. 22.58).

ask.q: In an isotropic medium where \(n_L = n_R\), what is the rotation angle \(\phi(z)\)?
ask.why: When \(n_L = n_R\), \(\phi(z) = 0\) and the plane of polarisation does not rotate (§22.8).

cards.label: 04 · §22.8 Worked example
cards.title: Worked example: optical rotation in quartz and turpentine (§22.8)
cards.body: For linearly polarised light (\(\lambda_0 = 0.6\,\mu\text{m} = 6000\text{ \AA}\)) propagating along the optic axis of quartz, \(|n_L - n_R| \approx 7\times 10^{-5}\), giving \(\phi = 21^\circ\) in \(z = 0.1\text{ cm}\) (\(1\text{ mm}\)). For turpentine, \(\phi = +37^\circ\) for \(z = 10\text{ cm}\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Rotating a Polaroid gives constant intensity, then adding a QWP gives extinction. The beam is:
cards.why: A QWP converts circularly polarised light into linearly polarised light, which then shows two zero minima through the rotating Polaroid (§22.7).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In an optically active medium, when is the substance dextro-rotatory (right-handed)?
cards.why: By Eq. (22.58), \(\phi(z) = (\pi/\lambda)(n_L - n_R)z > 0\) (dextro-rotatory) when \(n_L > n_R\) (§22.8).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: The normal modes of propagation in an optically active medium are LCP and ______ waves.
cards.why: In an optically active medium, the normal modes that propagate unchanged in polarisation state are LCP and RCP waves (§22.8).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: A quartz plate rotates polarisation by \(21^\circ\) per mm at \(6000\text{ \AA}\). Find rotation in degrees for \(3\text{ mm}\).
cards.why: Since optical rotation \(\phi(z)\) is directly proportional to thickness \(z\), \(\phi = 3 \times 21^\circ = 63^\circ\) (§22.8).

sheets.title: Q1 · Law of refraction (2 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 2 marks
cards.title: Question 1
cards.q: What is law of refraction ?
Coplanarity and Snell's sine formula

options.t: Both coplanarity and Snell's formula stated

cards.why: State both the plane condition and the sine ratio.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Snell's law of refraction
cards.body: Know first: Laws of reflection and refraction from Fermat's principle. The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal to the interface at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane. The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction equals the inverse ratio of the refractive indices, \( n_1 \sin\theta_1 = n_2 \sin\theta_2 \).

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Snell's law expression
cards.body: Relate the angles of incidence and refraction to the refractive indices of the two media. Coplanarity 1 · Snell's formula 1.

cards.q: In refraction, the incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in ____.
cards.why: Refraction at an interface is coplanar.

cards.q: According to Snell's law, the product \( n \sin\theta \) across an interface is ____.
cards.why: Snell's law states \(n1 \sin \theta1 = n2 \sin \theta2\).

cards.q: When light enters a medium of higher refractive index, it bends ____.
cards.why: Larger refractive index gives a smaller angle with the normal.

sheets.title: Q2 · Distance measurement in sign convention (2 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 2 marks
cards.title: Question 2
cards.q: According to sign convention how distances are measured ?
Origin P and longitudinal/transverse signs

options.t: Origin at pole P and right/left or up/down signs stated
Only right/left rule without origin stated

cards.why: Specify the pole as origin and the positive/negative directions.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Cartesian sign convention for distances
cards.body: Know first: Refraction and reflection at a single spherical surface. Taking the pole \( P \) of the surface as origin and rays incident from the left, all distances to the right of \( P \) are positive and distances to the left of \( P \) are negative. Distances measured upward perpendicular to the axis are positive and downward are negative.

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Sign of object, image and height distances
cards.body: Measure axial distances from the pole P and transverse distances perpendicular to the axis. Axial rule 1 · transverse rule 1.

cards.q: In the sign convention, the origin of coordinates is the ____.
cards.why: All axial distances are measured from the pole P.

cards.q: With light incident from the left, distances to the right of P are ____.
cards.why: Distances along the direction of incident light to the right of P are positive.

cards.q: Distances measured downward perpendicular to the principal axis are ____.
cards.why: Upward heights are positive and downward heights are negative.

sheets.title: Q3 · Definition of thin lens (2 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 2 marks
cards.title: Question 3
cards.q: Define a thin lens If the thickness is very small compared to the object and image distances, radii of curvature.
Spherical refracting medium and negligible thickness condition

options.t: Medium bounded by two spherical surfaces with \(t << |u\)|, |v|, |R| stated

cards.why: Define the bounding surfaces and the small-thickness condition.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Thin spherical lens
cards.body: Know first: The thin lens, principal foci and focal length. A medium bounded by two spherical refracting surfaces is called a thin spherical lens when its axial thickness \( t \) is very small compared to the object distance \( u \), image distance \( v \), and radii of curvature \( R_1, R_2 \). All axial distances can then be measured from the common optical center \( P \).

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Thin lens approximation
cards.body: Neglect the lens thickness t relative to u, v, R1 and R2 when adding the two surface refraction equations. Definition 1 · consequence 1.

cards.q: A spherical lens is bounded by two ____.
cards.why: A spherical lens has two spherical refracting boundaries.

cards.q: In a thin lens, all axial distances are measured from the ____.
cards.why: Because t is negligible, both poles coincide at the center P.

cards.q: The line joining the two centers of curvature of a lens is its ____.
cards.why: The line through C1 and C2 defines the axis of the lens.

sheets.title: Q4 · First focal length (2 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 2 marks
cards.title: Question 4
cards.q: Define first focal length.
Definition of first principal focus F1 and distance f1

options.t: Focus F1 for parallel emergent rays and distance f1 from lens stated
Only distance from lens stated without defining F1

cards.why: Define the first principal focus and its distance from the lens.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: First focal length f1
cards.body: Know first: The thin lens, principal foci and focal length. The first principal focus \( F_1 \) is the axial point such that rays passing through it (or appearing to pass through it) emerge parallel to the axis after refraction. The distance of \( F_1 \) from the lens is the first focal length \( f_1 \), which is negative for a converging lens and positive for a diverging lens.

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Condition for first focal length
cards.body: Set image distance v to infinity in the thin lens equation to obtain \(u = f1\). Definition 1 · formula/sign 1.

cards.q: Rays passing through the first principal focus emerge from the lens ____.
cards.why: An object at F1 forms an image at infinity.

cards.q: For a converging lens, the first focal length \( f_1 \) is ____.
cards.why: F1 lies to the left of a converging lens, so f1 is negative.

cards.q: When the same medium is on both sides of a thin lens, \( f_1 \) equals ____.
cards.why: For identical surrounding media, \(f1 = -f2 = -f\).

sheets.title: Q5 · Lateral magnification (2 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 2 marks
cards.title: Question 5
cards.q: Define lateral magnification.
Ratio of image height to object height and formula

options.t: Definition and formula \(m = y\)'/\(y = v/u\) given
Only verbal definition or only formula given

cards.why: State both the height ratio and the lens expression.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Lateral magnification m
cards.body: Know first: The Newton formula and lateral magnification. Lateral magnification \( m \) is defined as the ratio of the transverse height of the image \( y' \) to the height of the object \( y \). Positive \( m \) indicates an erect image and negative \( m \) indicates an inverted image.

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Lateral magnification expressions
cards.tex: m = \frac{y'}{y} = \frac{v}{u} \\ m = \frac{n_1 v}{n_2 u} \text{ (single spherical surface)}
cards.body: Relate image height to object height using similar triangles. Definition 1 · formula 1.

cards.q: Lateral magnification is the ratio of image height to ____.
cards.why: By definition, \(m = y\)'/y.

cards.q: A negative value of lateral magnification indicates an image that is ____.
cards.why: Opposite signs of y' and y mean the image is inverted.

cards.q: For a thin lens in air, lateral magnification \( m \) equals ____.
cards.why: From similar triangles at the optical center, \(m = v/u\).

sheets.title: Q6 · Bragg wavelength (2 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 2 marks
cards.title: Question 6
cards.q: Define Bragg wavelength.
Definition and Bragg condition formula

options.t: Wavelength satisfying constructive periodic reflection and formula given
Only formula or vague statement given

cards.why: State the constructive reflection condition and wavelength formula.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Bragg wavelength
cards.body: Know first: N-slit Fraunhofer diffraction pattern and grating. The Bragg wavelength is the wavelength strongly reflected by a periodic structure or crystal lattice of spacing \( d \) (or period \( \Lambda \)) when reflected waves interfere constructively. In general diffraction it obeys \( 2d\sin\theta = m\lambda_B \), and in a fiber Bragg grating \( \lambda_B = 2 n_{\text{eff}} \Lambda \).

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Bragg reflection condition
cards.body: Equate the path difference between successive periodic planes to an integral multiple of wavelength. Concept 1 · equation 1.

cards.q: Bragg reflection occurs when waves reflected from periodic planes interfere ____.
cards.why: Strong reflection requires constructive interference.

cards.q: In Bragg's law \( 2d\sin\theta = m\lambda \), the symbol \( d \) denotes ____.
cards.why: d is the separation between adjacent reflecting planes.

cards.q: For normal reflection in a Bragg grating of period \( \Lambda \), \( \lambda_B \) is ____.
cards.why: At normal incidence \(\sin \theta = 1\) and \(m = 1\).

sheets.title: Q7 · Angular divergence of circular aperture (2 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 2 marks
cards.title: Question 7
cards.q: Give the equation for angular divergence of diffraction of a circular aperture.
Airy disk angular radius formula and symbol meanings
cards.why: Write the \(1.22 \lambda / D\) equation and define D and \(\lambda\).

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Angular divergence of a circular aperture
cards.body: Know first: Single-slit Fraunhofer diffraction pattern. In Fraunhofer diffraction at a circular aperture of diameter \( D \) (or radius \( a \)), the angular half-width (divergence) of the central Airy disc to the first dark ring is \( \theta_1 \approx \frac{1.22\lambda}{D} \), where \( \lambda \) is the wavelength of light.

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: First dark ring angular radius
cards.body: State the angular radius of the first minimum of the Airy pattern and identify wavelength and aperture diameter. Equation 1 · symbols 1.

cards.q: The central bright disc in circular aperture diffraction is called the ____.
cards.why: Airy derived the circular aperture diffraction pattern.

cards.q: The numerical factor in \( \theta = 1.22\lambda / D \) for a circular aperture is ____.
cards.why: The first zero of J1(x) gives \(3.8317 / \pi = 1.22\).

cards.q: Increasing the diameter \( D \) of a circular aperture makes the angular divergence ____.
cards.why: Angular divergence is inversely proportional to aperture diameter D.

sheets.title: Q8 · Fresnel vs Fraunhofer diffraction (2 marks)
sheets.source: PYQ Nov 2023 Q8 · also Nov 2021 (CBCSS) Q6

cards.label: PYQ · 2 marks
cards.title: Question 8
cards.q: Differentiate Fresnel and Fraunhofer diffractions.
Source/screen distance and wavefront type

options.t: Both distance and wavefront differences stated

cards.why: Compare distances of source/screen and wavefront shapes.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Comparison of Fresnel and Fraunhofer diffraction
cards.body: Know first: Fresnel diffraction and zone plate. In Fresnel diffraction, the source, screen or both are at finite distances from the obstacle and the incident wavefronts are spherical or cylindrical without lenses. In Fraunhofer diffraction, the source and screen are effectively at infinite distances (achieved using collimating and focusing lenses) and the incident wavefronts are plane.
cards.tex: \text{Fresnel: finite distance; Fraunhofer: infinite distance (plane wavefronts)}

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Distinguishing criteria
cards.tex: \text{Fresnel: } R_{\text{source}}, R_{\text{screen}} \text{ finite (spherical/cylindrical wavefront)} \\ \text{Fraunhofer: } R_{\text{source}}, R_{\text{screen}} \to \infty \text{ (plane wavefront)}
cards.body: Contrast the source/screen distances and wavefront curvature. Distance criterion 1 · wavefront/lens criterion 1.

cards.q: In Fraunhofer diffraction, the wavefront incident on the aperture is ____.
cards.why: Collimated light from a source at infinity has plane wavefronts.

cards.q: In Fresnel diffraction, the source and screen are at ____.
cards.why: Fresnel is near-field diffraction at finite distances.

cards.q: Convex lenses are used in laboratory setups to observe ____.
cards.why: Lenses render the incident light parallel and focus parallel diffracted rays.

sheets.title: Q9 · Resolving power (2 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 2 marks
cards.title: Question 9
cards.q: Define resolving power.
Ability to separate close objects/wavelengths and expression
cards.why: Define resolving power and write its formula.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Resolving power of an optical instrument
cards.body: Know first: N-slit Fraunhofer diffraction pattern and grating. Resolving power is the ability of an optical instrument to form separate, distinguishable images of two closely spaced point objects or spectral lines. For a grating (chromatic resolving power), it is \( R = \frac{\lambda}{\Delta\lambda} = mN \), where \( m \) is the order and \( N \) is the total number of rulings.

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Grating and spatial resolving power
cards.body: State the definition of resolving power and the Rayleigh expression. Definition 1 · formula 1.

cards.q: Chromatic resolving power of a grating is defined as ____.
cards.why: Chromatic resolving power measures the smallest resolvable wavelength difference.

cards.q: According to Rayleigh's criterion, two images are just resolved when the principal maximum of one falls on the ____.
cards.why: Rayleigh's criterion places the maximum of one pattern at the first zero of the other.

cards.q: In the grating resolving power formula \( R = mN \), \( N \) is the ____.
cards.why: Resolving power depends on the total number of illuminated slits N.

sheets.title: Q10 · Polaroid (2 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 2 marks
cards.title: Question 10
cards.q: What is a polaroid ?
Aligned polymer sheet and selective absorption

options.t: Aligned long-chain polymer with iodine and selective absorption stated
Only states that it produces polarized light

cards.why: Describe the aligned polymer construction and dichroic action.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Polaroid sheet polarizer
cards.body: Know first: Production of linearly polarised light. A Polaroid is a plastic-like sheet containing aligned long-chain polymer molecules (such as polyvinyl alcohol doped with iodine) that conduct along their length. It absorbs the electric field component parallel to the molecular alignment and transmits the perpendicular component along its pass-axis to produce linearly polarized light.

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Selective absorption in a Polaroid
cards.tex: E_{\text{inc}} = E_{\parallel} + E_{\perp} \implies E_{\text{trans}} = E_{\perp} \\ I_{\text{trans}} = \frac{1}{2} I_0 \text{ (unpolarized input)}
cards.body: Conduction electrons along the iodine-doped polymer chains absorb the parallel component and pass the perpendicular component. Structure 1 · mechanism 1.

cards.q: In a Polaroid sheet, the electric field component parallel to the aligned polymer chains is ____.
cards.why: High conductivity along the iodine-doped chains dissipates the parallel component.

cards.q: The direction along which the transmitted electric vector oscillates in a Polaroid is its ____.
cards.why: The pass-axis is perpendicular to the aligned absorbing chains.

cards.q: Selective absorption of one polarization component in a material is called ____.
cards.why: Dichroic materials have different absorption coefficients for orthogonal polarizations.

sheets.title: Q11 · Analyser (2 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 2 marks
cards.title: Question 11
cards.q: Define analyser.
Role in detecting polarization and Malus's law variation

options.t: Second polarizing device used to detect state of polarization and intensity variation stated
Only states it is a polarizer

cards.why: Explain how rotating the second polarizer tests the polarization of light.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Analyser in polarization
cards.body: Know first: Effects of polariser and analyser; Malus's law. An analyser is a second polarizing device (such as a Polaroid or Nicol prism) placed in the path of a light beam to determine whether the beam is polarized and to find its plane of polarization. When rotated about the beam axis, the transmitted intensity of linearly polarized light varies as \( I = I_0 \cos^2\theta \), giving complete extinction twice per revolution.

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Action of an analyser
cards.body: Project the incident polarized amplitude onto the pass-axis of the analyser at angle \(\theta\). Definition 1 · Malus's law 1.

cards.q: A polarizing device used to test the state of polarization of a light beam is called an ____.
cards.why: The first device is the polarizer and the second is the analyser.

cards.q: When linearly polarized light is viewed through a rotating analyser, complete darkness occurs at ____.
cards.why: \(\cos^2(\theta) = 0\) at \(\theta = 90\) degrees and 270 degrees.

cards.q: The variation of transmitted intensity through an analyser is governed by ____.
cards.why: Malus's law gives \(I = I0 \cos^2(\theta)\).

sheets.title: Q12 · Requirements of holography (2 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 2 marks
cards.title: Question 12
cards.q: List the requirements of holography.
Coherent laser source, vibration-free table, high-resolution plate

options.t: Laser source, vibration isolation, high-resolution recording medium and beam splitter listed
Only one or two requirements listed

cards.why: List the four essential experimental requirements for recording a hologram.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Experimental requirements of holography
cards.body: Know first: Interference of light waves. Recording a hologram requires: (1) a highly coherent monochromatic light source such as a laser, (2) a beam splitter and mirrors to form reference and object beams, (3) a high-resolution photographic plate to record fine interference fringes, and (4) a vibration-free table so path differences remain stable within a fraction of \( \lambda \).

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Coherence and stability conditions
cards.tex: I = I_R + I_O + 2\sqrt{I_R I_O}\cos\delta \\ \text{Path difference } |L_O - L_R| < c\tau_c
cards.body: List the four experimental requirements needed for stationary interference fringes. Source & optics 1 · plate & stability 1.

cards.q: Holography requires a light source with high spatial and temporal ____.
cards.why: A laser provides the coherence needed for a stationary interference pattern.

cards.q: During hologram exposure, the optical table must be free from ____.
cards.why: Vibrations of even half a wavelength wash out the interference fringes.

cards.q: The photographic emulsion used in holography must have very high ____.
cards.why: Interference fringes are spaced on the order of a wavelength.

sheets.title: Q13 · Postulates of sign convention (5 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 5 marks
cards.title: Question 13
cards.q: Explain any four postulates of sign convention
Statement of four Cartesian sign convention postulates

options.t: Four postulates clearly stated with pole P as origin

cards.why: State four postulates from the standard sign convention.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Four postulates of the Cartesian sign convention
cards.body: Know first: Refraction and reflection at a single spherical surface. Taking the pole \( P \) as origin: (1) Rays are always incident from the left on the refracting or reflecting surface. (2) All axial distances to the right of \( P \) are positive and to the left of \( P \) are negative. (3) The acute angle a ray makes with the axis (or normal) is positive if the axis (or normal) rotates anticlockwise to coincide with the ray, and negative if clockwise. (4) All transverse distances measured upward perpendicular to the axis are positive and downward are negative.

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Summary of sign rules
cards.tex: 1.\; \text{Incident rays: left to right, origin at pole } P \\ 2.\; x > 0 \text{ right of } P, \quad x < 0 \text{ left of } P \\ 3.\; \theta > 0 \text{ anticlockwise from axis/normal, } \theta < 0 \text{ clockwise} \\ 4.\; y > 0 \text{ upward from axis, } y < 0 \text{ downward}
cards.body: List the incident direction, axial distance rule, angle rotation rule, and transverse height rule. Four postulates 4 · clarity/example 1.

cards.q: In the sign convention, incident rays always travel from ____.
cards.why: Rays are conventionally incident from the left on the optical surface.

cards.q: The angle between the axis and a ray is positive if the axis is rotated through an acute angle ____.
cards.why: Anticlockwise rotation from the reference line is taken as positive.

cards.q: For a real object placed in front (to the left) of a refracting surface, the object distance \( u \) is ____.
cards.why: Distances to the left of the pole P are negative.

sheets.title: Q14 · Intensity ratio for path difference lambda/3 (5 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 5 marks
cards.title: Question 14
cards.q: For an interference pattern, find the ratio of intensity at P to that at maximum such that path difference \(S_2P - S_1P = \lambda/3\).
Phase difference calculation and cosine-squared intensity ratio

options.t: Phase difference \(2\pi/3\) and intensity ratio \(I/I_{max} = 1/4\) found
Correct phase difference \(2\pi/3\) but arithmetic error in ratio

cards.why: Convert path difference to phase difference and evaluate \(\cos^2(\delta/2)\).

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Intensity ratio \(I / I_{max} = 1 / 4\)
cards.body: Know first: Interference of light waves. A path difference of \( \Delta = \lambda/3 \) corresponds to a phase difference \( \delta = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta = \frac{2\pi}{3} \). Using \( I = I_{\max}\cos^2(\delta/2) \), the ratio of the intensity at \( P \) to the maximum intensity is \( \cos^2(\pi/3) = \frac{1}{4} = 0.25 \).

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Intensity ratio from path difference
cards.body: Find the phase difference \(\delta\) from the path difference and substitute into the cosine-squared intensity law. Formula 1.5 · phase difference 1.5 · ratio 2.

cards.q: Phase difference \( \delta \) is related to path difference \( \Delta \) by ____.
cards.why: A path difference of \(\lambda\) corresponds to a phase difference of \(2 \pi\).

cards.q: For two equal-intensity coherent waves, resultant intensity \( I \) equals ____.
cards.why: Superposition of two equal waves gives \(I = 4 I0 \cos^2(\delta/2)\).

cards.q: When the path difference is \( \lambda/3 \), the ratio \( I/I_{\max} \) is ____.

sheets.title: Q15 · Fringe width in Young's double-hole experiment (5 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 5 marks
cards.title: Question 15
cards.q: In Young's double hole experiments, the distance between two holes is 0.5 mm, \(\lambda = 5 \times 10^{-5}\) cm and \(D = 50\) cm. What will be the fringe width?
Fringe width formula, unit conversion and numerical answer

options.t: Formula \(\beta = \lambda D / d\) and \(\beta = 0.05\) cm (0.5 mm) with units
Correct formula and substitution with minor unit/arithmetic slip

cards.why: Convert d, D, \(\lambda\) to consistent units and compute \(\beta = \lambda D / d\).

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Fringe width \(\beta = 0.05\) cm (0.5 mm)
cards.body: Know first: Interference of light waves. The fringe width in Young's double-hole experiment is \( \beta = \frac{\lambda D}{d} \). With \( d = 0.5\text{ mm} = 0.05\text{ cm} \), \( \lambda = 5\times 10^{-5}\text{ cm} \), and \( D = 50\text{ cm} \), we get \( \beta = 0.05\text{ cm} = 0.5\text{ mm} \).

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Calculation of fringe width
cards.tex: d = 0.5\text{ mm} = 0.05\text{ cm}, \quad \lambda = 5 \times 10^{-5}\text{ cm}, \quad D = 50\text{ cm} \\ \beta = \frac{\lambda D}{d} \\ \beta = \frac{5 \times 10^{-5} \times 50}{0.05} = 5 \times 10^{-2}\text{ cm} = 0.05\text{ cm} = 0.5\text{ mm}
cards.body: Substitute the given values in centimeters into the fringe-width formula. Formula 1.5 · substitution 1.5 · answer with units 2.

cards.q: In Young's double-slit experiment, fringe width \( \beta \) is given by ____.
cards.why: Fringe width is directly proportional to wavelength and screen distance, and inversely proportional to slit separation.

cards.q: If the distance between the two slits is halved, the fringe width becomes ____.
cards.why: \(\beta\) is inversely proportional to slit separation d.

cards.q: In Young's double-hole experiment, bright and dark fringes are ____.
cards.why: Fringe width \(\beta = \lambda D / d\) is independent of order n.

sheets.title: Q16 · Maxima and minima in N-slit Fraunhofer diffraction (5 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 5 marks
cards.title: Question 16
cards.q: Explain maxima and minima in an N slit Fraunhofer diffraction
Intensity formula, principal maxima, minima and secondary maxima

options.t: Intensity expression, principal maxima, \(N-1\) minima and \(N-2\) secondary maxima explained
Principal maxima and minima conditions stated without secondary maxima

cards.why: Give the N-slit intensity distribution and conditions for principal maxima, minima, and secondary maxima.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Principal maxima, minima and secondary maxima
cards.body: Know first: N-slit Fraunhofer diffraction pattern and grating. The intensity of an \( N \)-slit grating is \( I = I_0 \frac{\sin^2\beta}{\beta^2}\frac{\sin^2 N\gamma}{\sin^2\gamma} \), where \( \beta = \frac{\pi b\sin\theta}{\lambda} \) and \( \gamma = \frac{\pi d\sin\theta}{\lambda} \). Principal maxima of intensity \( N^2 I_0 \frac{\sin^2\beta}{\beta^2} \) occur when \( \gamma = m\pi \), i.e. \( d\sin\theta = m\lambda \). Between two adjacent principal maxima there are \( N - 1 \) minima where \( N\gamma = p\pi \) (\( p \neq mN \)) and \( N - 2 \) weak secondary maxima.
cards.tex: d\sin\theta = m\lambda \text{ (principal maxima)}, \quad N d\sin\theta = p\lambda \text{ (minima)}

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Conditions for N-slit extrema
cards.tex: I = I_0 \left(\frac{\sin\beta}{\beta}\right)^2 \left(\frac{\sin N\gamma}{\sin\gamma}\right)^2, \quad \beta = \frac{\pi b\sin\theta}{\lambda}, \quad \gamma = \frac{\pi d\sin\theta}{\lambda} \\ \text{Principal maxima: } \sin\gamma = 0 \implies \gamma = m\pi \implies d\sin\theta = m\lambda, \quad m = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \dots \\ \text{Minima: } \sin N\gamma = 0 \text{ with } \sin\gamma \neq 0 \implies N\gamma = p\pi \implies d\sin\theta = \frac{p}{N}\lambda \\ p \neq 0, \pm N, \pm 2N, \dots \implies (N-1)\text{ minima and }(N-2)\text{ secondary maxima}
cards.body: State the N-slit intensity equation and solve for zeros and indeterminate forms of the interference factor. Intensity formula 1.5 · principal maxima 1.5 · minima & secondary maxima 2.

cards.q: Between two adjacent principal maxima in an \( N \)-slit pattern, the number of minima is ____.
cards.why: p takes \(N-1\) integer values between mN and \((m+1)N\).

cards.q: Between two consecutive principal maxima of an \( N \)-slit grating, the number of secondary maxima is ____.
cards.why: There is one secondary maximum between each pair of the \(N-1\) minima.

cards.q: The peak intensity of the interference factor \( (\sin N\gamma / \sin\gamma)^2 \) at a principal maximum is ____.
cards.why: By L'Hopital's rule, lim \((\sin N \gamma / \sin \gamma)^2 = N^2\).

sheets.title: Q17 · Zone plate principle and construction (5 marks)
sheets.source: PYQ Nov 2023 Q17 · also Nov 2022 (CUCBCSS) Q21, Nov 2021 (CUCBCSS) Q21

cards.label: PYQ · 5 marks
cards.title: Question 17
cards.q: What is a zone plate. Explain
Definition, construction of concentric zones, and focal length formula

options.t: Definition, construction with radii proportional to \(\sqrt{n}\), and focal length formula explained
Construction and action as converging lens explained without full formula

cards.why: Explain how blocking alternate Fresnel half-period zones focuses light with multiple foci.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Fresnel zone plate
cards.body: Know first: Fresnel diffraction and zone plate. A zone plate is a specially constructed screen consisting of concentric circles whose radii are proportional to the square roots of natural numbers (\( r_n \propto \sqrt{n} \)), with alternate annular zones made opaque. By blocking either all even or all odd Fresnel half-period zones, the remaining zones interfere constructively at the focus, so the zone plate acts like a converging lens with multiple foci \( f_m = \frac{r_1^2}{(2m-1)\lambda} \).

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Zone radii and focal length
cards.tex: \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{n\lambda}{r_n^2} = \frac{1}{f_1} \\ r_n = \sqrt{n f_1 \lambda} = r_1 \sqrt{n} \\ A_{\text{res}} = A_1 + A_3 + A_5 + \dots \quad (\text{even zones blocked}) \\ f_m = \frac{r_1^2}{(2m-1)\lambda}, \quad m = 1, 2, 3, \dots
cards.body: Draw concentric circles of radii \(r1\cdot\sqrt{n}\), blacken alternate rings and photograph at reduced scale. Principle 2 · construction 1.5 · focal length formula 1.5.

cards.q: The radii of the concentric circles of a zone plate are proportional to the ____.
cards.why: The n-th half-period zone has radius rn = \(r1 \sqrt{n}\).

cards.q: Unlike a glass convex lens, a zone plate possesses ____.
cards.why: Higher-order foci occur at \(f1/3\), \(f1/5\), \(f1/7\), etc.

cards.q: The principal focal length \( f_1 \) of a zone plate is equal to ____.
cards.why: Since \(r1 = \sqrt{f1 \lambda}\), we have \(f1 = r1^2 / \lambda\).

sheets.title: Q18 · Huygens' explanation of double refraction (5 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 5 marks
cards.title: Question 18
cards.q: Define and explain Huygen's explanation of double refraction
Definition of double refraction and Huygens' spherical/ellipsoidal wavelets

options.t: Splitting into o-ray and e-ray defined, and spherical + ellipsoidal wave surfaces explained with optic axis
Double refraction defined and wavelets mentioned without positive/negative crystal detail
Only definition of double refraction given

cards.why: Define double refraction and explain Huygens' secondary spherical (o-wave) and ellipsoidal (e-wave) wave surfaces.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Double refraction and Huygens' wave theory
cards.body: Know first: Double refraction and Huygens' explanation. Double refraction (birefringence) is the splitting of an unpolarized light beam entering an anisotropic crystal (like calcite or quartz) into two linearly polarized beams: the ordinary ray (o-ray), which obeys Snell's law, and the extraordinary ray (e-ray), which generally does not. According to Huygens, each point in a uniaxial crystal emits two secondary wave surfaces: a sphere of speed \( v_o = c/n_o \) for the o-ray and an ellipsoid of revolution for the e-ray touching the sphere along the optic axis.

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Huygens' ray velocity surfaces
cards.tex: v_{ro} = \frac{c}{n_o} \quad (\text{sphere for o-ray}) \\ \frac{1}{v_{re}^2} = \frac{\cos^2\theta}{(c/n_o)^2} + \frac{\sin^2\theta}{(c/n_e)^2} \quad (\text{ellipsoid of revolution for e-ray}) \\ \theta = 0 \text{ (along optic axis)}: \; v_{re} = v_{ro} = \frac{c}{n_o} \\ \theta = \frac{\pi}{2}: \; v_{re} = \frac{c}{n_e} \quad (n_e < n_o \Rightarrow v_{re} > v_{ro} \text{ negative; } n_e > n_o \Rightarrow v_{re} < v_{ro} \text{ positive})
cards.body: Define o-ray and e-ray, write their velocity equations, and compare the spherical and ellipsoidal wave surfaces. Definition 1.5 · Huygens postulates 2 · positive/negative crystals 1.5.

cards.q: In Huygens' theory of double refraction, the secondary wave surface for the ordinary ray is a ____.
cards.why: The ordinary ray travels with the same velocity \(c/n_o\) in all directions.

cards.q: Along the optic axis of a uniaxial crystal, the velocities of the o-ray and e-ray are ____.
cards.why: The sphere and ellipsoid touch each other along the optic axis.

cards.q: In a negative uniaxial crystal like calcite, the ellipsoid of revolution lies ____.
cards.why: For a negative crystal \(n_e < n_o\), so \(v_{re} >= v_{ro}\) and the ellipsoid encloses the sphere.

sheets.title: Q19 · Applications of holography in diverse fields (5 marks)
sheets.source: PYQ Nov 2023 Q19 · also Nov 2022 (CBCSS) Q10, Nov 2021 (CBCSS) Q18

cards.label: PYQ · 5 marks
cards.title: Question 19
cards.q: Explain holography in diverse fields.
Explanation of at least four major applications of holography

options.t: Four or more applications (interferometry/NDT, data storage, microscopy, security, optical elements) explained

cards.why: Explain how holography is applied across engineering, data storage, microscopy, and security.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Applications of holography
cards.body: Know first: Interference of light waves. Holography is used in: (1) Holographic interferometry for non-destructive testing (NDT) of micro-strains, vibrations and defects by superposing stressed and unstressed wavefields; (2) High-density 3D optical data storage in volume crystals; (3) Holographic microscopy and particle-size analysis to focus through 3D volumes after recording; and (4) Anti-counterfeiting security holograms and holographic optical elements (scanners, gratings).

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Storage capacity and interferometric sensitivity
cards.body: Describe four distinct applications across industry, computing, medicine/microscopy and security. Four applications explained 4 · clarity 1.

cards.q: Double-exposure holographic interferometry is widely used for ____.
cards.why: Interference between two exposures reveals minute surface deformations without damaging the object.

cards.q: A hologram records both the amplitude and the ____.
cards.why: Interference with the reference beam encodes the phase into fringe positions.

cards.q: Even if a hologram is broken into small pieces, each piece can reconstruct the ____.
cards.why: Every point on the object scatters light across the whole holographic plate.

sheets.title: Q20 · Gaussian formula and reflection at a single spherical surface (10 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 10 marks
cards.title: Question 20
cards.q: Write and explain the Gaussian formula for a single spherical surface. With figure explain the reflection by a single spherical surface.
Gaussian formula for refraction at a single spherical surface

options.t: Formula \(n2/v - n1/u = (n2-n1)/R\) stated and paraxial derivation/explanation given
Formula stated with brief explanation of symbols

cards.why: Write and explain the Gaussian refraction equation and its sign convention.

cards.q: Ray diagram and derivation of reflection at a single spherical surface

options.t: Neat ray diagram and complete paraxial derivation of \(1/u + 1/v = 2/R\)

cards.why: Draw the spherical mirror ray diagram and derive the mirror equation.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Gaussian refraction formula and spherical mirror equation
cards.body: Know first: Refraction and reflection at a single spherical surface. For paraxial refraction at a spherical surface of radius \( R \) separating media \( n_1 \) and \( n_2 \), the Gaussian formula is \( \frac{n_2}{v} - \frac{n_1}{u} = \frac{n_2 - n_1}{R} \). For reflection at a spherical mirror \( SPM \), using \( \phi_1 = \phi_2 \) and small-angle approximations \( \phi_1 = \beta - \alpha_1 \approx \frac{h}{r} - \frac{h}{x} \) and \( \phi_2 = \alpha_2 - \beta \approx \frac{h}{y} - \frac{h}{r} \) with \( u = -x, v = -y, R = -r \), we obtain \( \frac{1}{u} + \frac{1}{v} = \frac{2}{R} \).

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Gaussian refraction and spherical reflection derivation
